claims.text: The structural and chemical stability of multimetallic nanoparticles is governed by the balance between configurational entropy, atomic size mismatch, and mixing enthalpy.
High configurational entropy stabilizes a single-phase solid solution.
Atomic size mismatch can destabilize the solid solution and drive phase segregation at elevated temperatures.
Adverse mixing enthalpies can destabilize the solid solution and drive phase segregation at elevated temperatures.
The initial nanoparticles contain five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and form a single-phase solid solution at room temperature.
Systematically varying elemental composition can modulate atomic size mismatch while retaining high configurational entropy.
At lower temperatures, configurational entropy maintains the single-phase structure.
Upon increasing temperature, sufficiently large atomic size mismatch or unfavorable mixing enthalpy outweighs the stabilizing effect of configurational entropy.
The proposed destabilization mechanism leads to phase separation.
The proposed destabilization mechanism leads to chemical ordering.
Nanoparticles with minimal atomic size mismatch will largely retain a single-phase structure and homogeneous elemental distribution.
Nanoparticles with larger atomic size mismatch will show more phase segregation than nanoparticles with minimal mismatch.
Nanoparticles with larger atomic size mismatch will show stronger chemical-ordering trends, particularly near 1923 K.
The prediction applies from 473 K to 1923 K in both inert and reactive catalytic or thermoelectric environments.
The temperature at which segregation begins depends on atomic size mismatch and mixing-enthalpy differences.
The extent of segregation depends on composition and environmental factors.
